transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2026-01-15
- Start: 16:30 PST
- Duration: ~58 mins
- Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Alvarez (CTO - Verdant Bio), Dana Kim (Lead SRE - Verdant), Sara Lee (Product)

Summary:
Verdant Bio is evaluating Redwood for a primary inference path for their internal research and customer-facing annotation products. Main focus on reliability, incident tolerance and multi-region fallbacks. They are weighing Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private given PII/PHI concerns on some workloads. Key asks: how do Redwood fallbacks work (model variants, regions, capacity tiers), SLA guarantees for Dedicated, audit/KMS/SSO controls for Private, and a benchmark run to validate tail latency under burst traffic.

Topics discussed:
- Fallback policies and automatic model variants
- Multi-region routing and geo-residency
- SLA expectations and Dedicated latency/uptime targets
- Security (SOC2, KMS, SSO) and audit logs
- Benchmark plan and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. This is Alex from Redwood, AE on the account, and Priya is our SE. How's it going Mark, Dana?
[00:08] Mark: Good, thanks. We're excited to dig in. We — sorry, quick note — some of our data is considered sensitive so we wanna make sure we understand Private options, but also cost is a big factor.
[00:17] Priya: Yeah absolutely, we can cover Hosted, Dedicated, and Private and the routing/fallback story across them. Just to set expectations, today's goal is to capture your SLOs and failure modes so we can propose a benchmark and config.
[00:28] Dana: Great. We get fairly spiky bursts from our annotation tool — like 5x baseline QPS for a couple minutes, then back down. We need to maintain 95th percentile latency under 250ms for short responses, and keep system availability — if there's a region outage we need automatic fallback within the same continent ideally.
[00:45] Alex: Got it. To walk through high-level: Redwood has smart routing, you can set policies by latency, cost, or region. We also support automatic fallback to compatible model variants — e.g., a lower-memory quantized variant, or a model in a different region — plus capacity tiers (burst pools) on Dedicated.
[01:03] Mark: How deterministic is that? Like we need predictable failover, not random slowdowns. If you route to a quantized model with slightly lower quality, we need observability to see regression and a way to rollback.
[01:18] Priya: Totally. Our rollout and routing layer supports canary and A/B policies. You can define a policy that says: if p95 > X or error rate > Y for N minutes, automatically fail over to a fallback route that points to a specific model variant. We also emit token-level latency and per-route error metrics to the Console and to your logging endpoint.
[01:38] Dana: And in practice, how fast is the switch? We can't afford long cache warmups causing large latency spikes.
[01:45] Priya: There are two parts: routing decision and runtime warmup. Routing decision is immediate — the control plane flips to the fallback route — but the runtime might need to load KV cache or initialize a model shard. For that reason Dedicated supports pre-warmed burst capacity and persistent model velocity in memory so failover is near-instant — like tens to low hundreds of ms for routing and cold start if pre-warmed, otherwise could be seconds.
[02:10] Mark: Okay, we probably need pre-warmed. For Private, how much control do we get over autoscaling and pre-warm?
[02:18] Alex: In Private, you manage the infra so you set autoscaling and keep pools warm; Redwood's control plane can still orchestrate rollouts. For Dedicated, we offer configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity options. We can propose a Dedicated pool with guaranteed warm nodes for your critical routes.
[02:33] Sara: Quick Q — what about multi-region? We need EU and US routing and data residency for EU workloads. If a primary EU region has an incident, can traffic fail over to another EU region first, then to US if needed?
[02:47] Priya: Yes — routing policies are tiered. You can set region preferences and fallthrough. Typical policy: prefer eu-west-1, then eu-central-1, then us-west-2 as last resort. You can also configure data residency constraints so certain routes never leave a region.
[03:05] Dana: Are there scenarios where Redwood will automatically cross borders for capacity? That's a dealbreaker for us.
[03:12] Alex: We don't cross borders if you've configured residency constraints. Default behavior is to favor same-region or same-continent to minimize cross-border traffic, but a policy can be set to allow cross-region failover in emergencies if you opt in.
[03:26] Mark: OK good. Then about SLA — what do you guarantee for Dedicated? We need to know uptime and latency SLOs and credits.
[03:34] Alex: Our Dedicated SLA for uptime is 99.95% for the control plane and 99.9% for serving endpoints in the committed pool. Latency SLOs are provided as targets (e.g., 95th percentile under X ms) depending on the model and sequence length; we publish verified performance profiles for our curated models. SLA credits are standard — pro-rata service credits for downtime beyond SLA. We'll include the exact SLA language in the contract.
[03:58] Dana: Is that per-route or per-cluster? We need per-route guarantees for our critical annotation pipeline.
[04:04] Priya: We can map routes to reserved capacity so you get predictable throughput and latency for those routes. The SLA would apply to the reserved pool backing those routes.
[04:12] Mark: And monitoring — we need audit logs and KMS integrations. Our security team will want to see SSO and RBAC mappings and HSM/KMS usage for key encryption.
[04:22] Alex: For Private we integrate with customer KMS and HSM. For Dedicated and Hosted we offer KMS integrations and server-side encryption; we can discuss HSM on the enterprise plan. We support SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and audit logs with configurable retention. I'll send the security whitepaper and SOC2 cert.
[04:39] Sara: Do you support per-request correlation IDs? That'd help our tracing.
[04:43] Priya: Yes, you can pass trace IDs; we include tracing hooks and per-request metadata in logs.
[04:48] Mark: Let's talk about the failure modes — what happens on a hardware failure in a region?
[04:53] Priya: If it's a hardware failure on a node, requests are automatically sharded to other healthy nodes; the KV cache might get invalidated for some sessions but we have persistent checkpointing in Dedicated. For region-level failure, routing policy will failover to the preferred fallback region; if that region has pre-warmed capacity you'll see minimal disruption.
[05:11] Dana: What's the typical observed tail latency during a failover? We've seen 95th jump to multiple seconds during other vendor failovers.
[05:19] Priya: If pre-warmed capacity exists, tail uplift is small — maybe a few hundred ms. If we require cold-starting models or need to pull artifacts from storage, it could be seconds. That's why we recommend pre-warming critical models and keeping a small warm buffer.
[05:33] Alex: We also support model variants — e.g., route to a smaller, quantized model as an immediate fallback while a full model comes up. That reduces cost and warmup time but you trade off some quality.
[05:43] Mark: How do you measure quality regressions? We need to tie regression alerts to our eval set and prompt suite.
[05:49] Priya: Redwood Optimize integrates quality monitoring; you can upload eval prompts and set regression thresholds. If fallback is triggered, Optimize can run quick checks against your prompts and alert if quality drops below threshold.
[05:59] Dana: Ok that sounds promising. For the benchmark, we want to simulate our spiky traffic and a region outage during a spike. Can Redwood run that or do we run it?
[06:08] Priya: We can run it jointly — we'll provide a runbook. We'll need your traffic profile and sample payloads, plus the target models. We can run against Hosted and Dedicated configs to show differences in tail latency and failover behavior.
[06:21] Mark: One more — cost controls. If we enable cross-region failover to US in case EU is down, what's the cost impact? We don't want surprise bills.
[06:29] Alex: Routing policies have cost tags and you can set caps. You can also set budget-based failover rules or require manual approval for cross-region failover. We'll show cost delta in the Console so you can see per-route cost by region.
[06:44] Sara: Our security team will also ask about data retention and deletion — logs, cache, and usage metadata.
[06:50] Alex: Retention is configurable; for Private you control retention. For Hosted and Dedicated we offer configurable retention and deletion policies and can include callbacks for deletion requests. We'll include details in the security package.
[06:59] Dana: For Dedicated, what does the commitment look like? We prefer a reserved pool with burst capacity, what's the typical lead time?
[07:06] Alex: Lead time depends on the size and region but typically 2-4 weeks to provision dedicated GPUs and reserve warm capacity; for urgent needs we can often provision faster with partner capacity.
[07:16] Mark: If we start Hosted for some routes and then move to Dedicated for high-throughput, is migration smooth?
[07:22] Priya: Yes, the API and routing abstractions are the same across Hosted/Dedicated/Private. You can pin model versions and swap the underlying backing capacity with minimal changes to your application.
[07:33] Alex: Recap of our asks: Verdant to send traffic profile and SLOs, Redwood to send security docs and pricing, Redwood SE to propose benchmark plan.
[07:42] Mark: Correct. Also want to include our legal team early for any cross-border clauses.
[07:47] Alex: We'll loop legal in the next step.
[07:50] Sara: One last quick nit — do you have standard playbooks for incident communication? We need runbooks.
[07:55] Priya: Yes, we have incident runbooks and on-call processes for Dedicated customers; we'll include those in the package.
[08:02] Mark: Alright, that covers our main concerns. Thanks.
